text: One of the generally agreed upon features of morality. <break time="0.8s" /> Is that it involves actions perceived to be binding on people. <break time="0.8s" /> This is the ought or should quality of morality. <break time="0.8s" /> That is the subject of a variety of types of philosophical analyses. <break time="0.8s" /> Many moral philosophers have been concerned. <break time="0.8s" /> With ways of characterizing procedures, judgments, and reasoning. <break time="0.8s" /> That lead to a sense of obligation. <break time="0.8s" /> In that case. <break time="0.8s" /> Judgments about obligations can be compatible. <break time="0.8s" /> With opposition and resistance to cultural practices. <break time="0.8s" /> And to the ways individuals are treated by society. <break time="0.8s" /> By contrast. <break time="0.8s" /> In much of the field of psychology. <break time="0.8s" /> The sense of ought or obligation. <break time="0.8s" /> Not surprisingly. <break time="0.8s" /> Has been psychologized. <break time="0.8s" /> In the sense that there is a search. <break time="0.8s" /> For psychological mechanisms. <break time="0.8s" /> That produce changes. <break time="0.8s" /> Involving accommodations to the values, norms, and practices of society. <break time="0.8s" /> Morality, then. <break time="0.8s" /> Is basically a form of compliance. <break time="0.8s" /> That becomes part of the individual. <break time="0.8s" /> Through the formation of, as examples. <break time="0.8s" /> Habits, conscience, or traits of character. <break time="0.8s" /> In that context. <break time="0.8s" /> Opposition and resistance would be viewed. <break time="0.8s" /> As that which comes from the assertion. <break time="0.8s" /> Of nonmoral or immoral individual drives. <break time="0.8s" /> Needs, interests, and desires.
